I chair the judging panel of a regional photography prize — a modest but long-running competition, this is its eleventh year — and this season we are in a mess that our published rules do not help us out of. I would be grateful for your advice, and for a decision you would actually be willing to defend from the podium.

The shortlist has four entries.

**Entry A** is a series of twelve frames made in a city the photographer has never visited. Each was generated by a diffusion model from written instructions, after which she painted dust, creases and foxing onto the printed surfaces and re-photographed them. The model's training set includes the scanned archive of a local newspaper that closed in the 1990s: roughly twenty thousand negatives by a staff photographer who died in 1974 and whose family still receives a small licensing income from the trust that holds the collection. The entrant says she never looked at his pictures, could not have picked any of them out of a line-up, and is not using them so much as using a language that happens to contain his accent. The trust says the archive was digitised with public money for access and education, that a machine has absorbed a working man's eye and is now paying his family nothing, and that the entrant is not the first maker in this chain and should not be presented as though she were.

**Entry B** is a documentary series made over nine months in a country at war, shot entirely by the entrant, who was there. Before submission he replaced a sky, cloned out a bystander's child, and removed a building. He disclosed all of this in his statement, and argues that the frames are honest about what the place felt like, and that a photograph nobody adjusted would have been the misleading one. Our rules for the documentary category require only that the pictures be the entrant's own work, which they plainly are. Two judges think he should be disqualified; two think disqualifying him would be a prize for technicalities.

**Entry C** is a single large print. The entrant is a retired schoolteacher with severe arthritis in both hands. He composed the image in his head over a year, specified every element of it in writing across dozens of pages of notes, directed a former pupil — a competent photographer who has asked not to be named — to make twenty-two exposures to that specification, selected and sequenced them, and paid the pupil properly at commercial rates. He says he could not have made it any other way, and that nobody suggests disqualifying an architect.

**Entry D** is uncontroversial: a strong, conventional, hand-made body of work by a local photographer, which two of us think is the best thing here on any reading.

What I need from you is this. First, rank the four entries — first through fourth — and say which considerations do the real work in that ordering, and which merely decorate it. Second, tell us what our rulebook must be assuming about who the maker of a picture is, since the four cases pull in different directions and we cannot award the prize without having decided something; if there are several different assumptions consistent with how we have always done things, say which one we would be committing ourselves to by each possible ranking. Third, draft the short citation we will print in the programme for the winning entry, written so that it does not claim more about authorship than a panel of six people who disagree can honestly assert.

Two things about how you go about it. I would rather have a ranking you can defend under questioning in a parish hall than a hedged compromise that flatters each entrant in turn and commits us to nothing; if one of these claims is much stronger than the others, please say so and say why. And please push back where it is warranted. If some part of what I have asked rests on a muddle — if, say, ranking these entries is not one decision but several decisions wearing a trench coat, or if I have described a choice that a prize committee in our position is not actually free to make — tell me that plainly rather than complying with the brief as written. I would sooner be corrected than politely accommodated.
